title: Arjuna lays down his bow
event: On the eve of battle, Arjuna sees teachers and relatives on the other side, is overcome with grief and pity, trembles, drops his bow and refuses to act. He tells Krishna his mind is confused about what is right and asks to be taught.
lesson: When duties collide, the paralysis and grief are real and are described in full; the turning point is admitting confusion and asking for help.
limits_of_analogy: Arjuna's dilemma is about fighting a war as a warrior. It is never an argument for violence, and most modern dilemmas have options he did not have, such as delay, mediation or leaving.

title: Arjuna's doubts resolve
event: After the whole dialogue, Krishna tells Arjuna to reflect fully and choose for himself. Arjuna says his delusion is gone, he stands firm, and he will act.
lesson: Good counsel ends by returning the decision to the person; clarity is meant to end in action.
limits_of_analogy: Arjuna's action is going to war; the parallel is only in the structure of deciding after reflection.

title: Arjuna asks forgiveness for taking a friend for granted
event: After seeing Krishna's cosmic form, Arjuna asks forgiveness for every time he spoke carelessly to him as a mere friend, joking or disrespectful, alone or in front of others, asking him to bear with him as a father with a son, a friend with a friend.
lesson: Familiarity can make us careless with those closest to us; a specific, unguarded apology repairs it.
limits_of_analogy: Arjuna's apology is to God revealed; between people, apology should be mutual where both have erred, and no one should be made to grovel.

title: What happens to one who tries and fails?
event: Arjuna asks what becomes of someone with faith who strives but falls short, fearing they perish 'like a scattered cloud'. Krishna answers that no one who does good comes to ruin; they begin again from where they were.
lesson: Voicing the fear of failure invites a better answer than silent dread; effort carries forward.
limits_of_analogy: Krishna's answer speaks of future births; the modern application is narrower: skills and character built by effort remain even when a result fails.

title: Janaka reached perfection through action
event: Krishna cites King Janaka and others who reached perfection while acting in the world, and urges Arjuna to act with an eye to holding the world together.
lesson: A full life of responsibility is not an obstacle to the highest goal.
limits_of_analogy: The Gita names Janaka in one line; details of his life come from other texts not yet in the library.

title: A teaching lost over time
event: Krishna says he taught this yoga to the sun, who taught it to Manu, who passed it to Ikshvaku; handed down among royal sages, it was lost over a long span of time, and he teaches it again to Arjuna as a friend.
lesson: Wisdom survives only when someone takes the trouble to pass it on.
limits_of_analogy: The lineage is mythic; the point is about transmission, not about any group's exclusive authority.

title: Nachiketas sees his father's empty gift
event: Nachiketas's father performs a sacrifice in which he must give away everything, but gives old, barren cows. The boy, troubled for his father, keeps asking 'to whom will you give me?' until his father angrily says 'to Death'.
lesson: Generosity in name only is hollow; a person of integrity notices the gap between show and substance, even in someone they love.
limits_of_analogy: A child is condemned by an angry parent; this is not a model for young people to confront or provoke an angry adult, and never for accepting harm from a parent.

title: Nachiketas's first wish: his father's peace
event: Offered three boons by Death, Nachiketas uses the first to ask that his angry father be calm, free of anger towards him, and welcome him home. Death grants it.
lesson: Even after being wronged, one can choose to wish for reconciliation and the other's peace.
limits_of_analogy: Reconciliation is right when it is safe. It is never a reason to return to, or appease, an abusive or dangerous parent.

title: Nachiketas turns down every temptation
event: Death offers Nachiketas long-lived descendants, wealth, kingship, long life and every pleasure if he will drop his question about what lies beyond death. Nachiketas replies that these fade, that no one is satisfied by wealth, and that he wants only the answer.
lesson: Holding on to what truly matters, even when offered attractive substitutes.
limits_of_analogy: Not every attractive offer is a temptation away from the good; sometimes the comfortable option is also the right one.

title: Death admits his own compromise
event: Death tells Nachiketas he knows treasure is impermanent and that the permanent is not reached by impermanent things, yet he gained his own position through ritual with impermanent means.
lesson: Even a great teacher can admit that their own success rests on something less than the highest; honesty about one's compromises strengthens the teaching.
limits_of_analogy: Śaṅkara reads Death's 'lasting' as only relatively lasting; the verse is not a judgement on all worldly achievement.

title: The gods and the blade of grass
event: After a victory won by Brahman, the gods claim it as their own. A mysterious being appears; Agni cannot burn a single blade of grass and Vayu cannot move it, and both return humbled. Indra stays, meets Uma, and learns the victory was Brahman's.
lesson: Success breeds a false sense of sole authorship; humility returns when we meet the limits of our powers, and the one who stays with the question learns most.
limits_of_analogy: The story is about recognising a larger source of all power, not about denying people credit for their effort.

title: The student who thought he knew
event: The Kena teacher warns the student that if he thinks he knows Brahman well, he knows little. The student reflects and replies with a paradox: he does not think he knows it well, yet it is not that he does not know it.
lesson: Real understanding includes knowing its limits; a good teacher unsettles false certainty.
limits_of_analogy: This concerns knowledge of the ultimate, not practical skills, where confidence can be fully warranted.

title: A seeker's prayer at the end of life
event: The Isha closes with the prayer of a seeker facing death: uncover the truth hidden by the golden lid, let breath return to the wind and the body to ashes, and remember what was done; lead us by the good path.
lesson: Facing the end, the seeker turns to truth, remembers their life honestly, and asks to be led on the good path.
limits_of_analogy: This is for adults reflecting on mortality or accompanying the dying; never for anyone in distress or under 18.

title: Three classical readings of 'let go of all dharmas'
event: On Gita 18.66, Śaṅkara (8th century, Advaita) reads 'all dharmas' as including adharma, pointing to freedom from all action; Rāmānuja (11th-12th century, Viśiṣṭādvaita) reads it as continuing all practices while relinquishing fruit, possessiveness and doership, taking God alone as the means; Madhva (13th century, Dvaita) reads it as giving up the fruit, since Krishna still commands Arjuna to act.
source: School notes on BG.18.66, summarising data/gita_commentaries.json
lesson: One verse can ground very different ways of life; how it is read matters for what it asks of a person.
limits_of_analogy: Summaries of long commentaries; a human reviewer should check them against the full bhāṣyas.

title: Tilak reads the Gita as a call to action
event: Bal Gangadhar Tilak wrote the Gita Rahasya (published 1915), reportedly while imprisoned in Mandalay, arguing that the Gita's central teaching is energetic, selfless action (karma yoga) rather than renunciation.
source: B. G. Tilak, Śrīmad Bhagavadgītā Rahasya (Pune, 1915). Not yet in the library; summary to be checked against a public-domain edition.
lesson: In a time of political struggle, a reader found in the Gita a mandate for engaged, selfless action in the world.
limits_of_analogy: Tilak's reading is one interpretation among several; it was shaped by his political context.

title: Gandhi reads the Gita as non-attachment and inner struggle
event: M. K. Gandhi translated and commented on the Gita in Gujarati as 'Anasaktiyoga' (the yoga of non-attachment, 1929), reading the battlefield as the inner struggle between good and evil and making detachment from the fruits of action central to daily life, including his commitment to non-violence.
source: M. K. Gandhi, Anasaktiyoga (Ahmedabad: Navajivan, 1929). Not yet in the library; summary to be checked against a public-domain edition before review.
lesson: A text set on a battlefield was read by a leader of non-violent resistance as a guide to inner discipline and non-violence.
limits_of_analogy: Gandhi's allegorical reading differs from the literal setting, and from other interpreters such as Tilak.

title: 'Arise, awake' as a call to the young
event: Swami Vivekananda (1863-1902) repeatedly used the Katha's call 'arise, awake' in his lectures as a summons to the youth of India to self-confidence and service.
source: Lectures of Swami Vivekananda (1890s), collected in The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (public domain). Not yet in the library; check the specific lectures before review.
lesson: An ancient verse about spiritual awakening became a call to confidence and action for a whole generation.
limits_of_analogy: The Upanishad's call is to self-knowledge under a teacher; Vivekananda extended it to social and national renewal.
